title: The Secret to Leading Inexperienced Team Members
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece challenges the intuitive approach of teaching inexperienced team members the 'rules of the game' before letting them act, arguing that this well-meaning strategy actually paralyzes them. The author distinguishes between knowing what NOT to do and knowing what TO do. The recommended approach inverts the typical order: give inexperienced team members small, directed actions to execute first, and let the context come later, once they've built some confidence through action and feedback.
points: Teaching inexperienced team members the rules before they act often paralyzes them rather than preparing them.
The piece distinguishes 'telling' from 'directing', arguing the latter is what inexperienced people actually need first.
Getting a novice into small, directed action first is described as what actually opens their ability to learn.
This approach inverts the common assumption that context and explanation should come before action.
quotes: There is a world of difference between knowing what NOT to do versus knowing what to do and doing it. Inexperienced team members need one thing more than any other from those who lead them: the direction to act.
When a leader tells an inexperienced team member what not to do or explains the conventions surrounding the game, the person can become paralyzed.
Counterintuitively, directed action is what inexperienced team members need most.
Instead of providing inexperienced team members with the context to succeed, they give them small actions to execute.
Telling them just creates confusion. Showing them is not yet possible. Directing them in given actions and tactics is what opens the mind and enhances the learning process.
